title: 1. Knead the clay
plain: Treat the clay like bread dough. Knead it so it is smooth and has no hidden air pockets.
why: If you skip this, little air holes can make a piece crack later.
doneWhen: You cut it open and the inside looks smooth and one color — no crumbs, no holes.
body: Knead the clay first, like dough. That pushes out air and makes it even. Skip it, and bubbles can make a piece fail later.
steps: Press the clay into a ball.
Push it forward with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it, and do that again.
After a minute, cut it in half. Dry crumbs or holes mean keep going.
Stop when the inside looks smooth.

terms.meaning: The studio word for this kneading. Same thing as what you just did.

ask: How do I know I have kneaded enough?

video.title: Watch how to knead clay and check for air bubbles

title: 2. Make a small bowl
plain: Your first piece: a little bowl you shape with your thumb and fingers. No wheel needed.
why: This teaches even thickness — the skill every later project uses.
doneWhen: The sides are about as thick as your pinky all the way around, and the top edge is smooth.
body: Make a ball. Push your thumb in, then pinch and turn so the sides stay even. Stop when they are about as thick as your pinky.
steps: Roll a ball that fits in your palm.
Press your thumb into the middle — not all the way through the bottom.
Pinch the clay between your thumb (inside) and fingers (outside).
Turn the ball a little after each pinch so one side does not get thin.
Stop when the sides are about a pinky thick.
Smooth the top edge with a slightly wet finger.

terms.meaning: A bowl made by pinching, not by a wheel.

ask: My bowl is thicker on one side. How do I fix that?

video.title: Watch how to pinch a small bowl with air-dry clay

title: 3. Stick two pieces together
plain: Clay does not glue itself if you just mash two pieces. Scratch both sides, add a little clay-water paste, then press.
why: Handles and extra bits fall off when this step is skipped.
doneWhen: The seam is blended and you cannot easily wiggle the new piece off.
body: Scratch both sides, brush on clay mixed with water, press, and smooth the join. If a handle falls off later, the join was dry or you skipped the scratching.
steps: Scratch a criss-cross on both surfaces with a fork.
Mix a pea of clay with a few drops of water until it is like yogurt. Brush that on the scratches.
Press the pieces together and wiggle them slightly.
Smooth the join with a finger so it looks like one piece.

terms.meaning: Scratch the surface so the join has grip.
Clay mixed with water — the paste that acts like glue.

ask: Why did my handle fall off?

title: 4. Build a cup with clay snakes
plain: Roll snakes of clay, stack them on a base, and blend them into a cup.
why: You can make something taller than a small bowl without a wheel.
doneWhen: The inside is blended smooth (no tunnels) and the cup can sit without wobbling.
body: Roll even snakes. If they squash flat, the clay is too wet. Scratch and paste every join. Blend the inside first so it is strong.
steps: Make a small bowl or a pancake for the base.
Roll a snake of even thickness on a dry table.
Scratch the base, brush on clay-water paste, lay the snake on, and press.
Add snakes one by one. Blend the inside so there are no gaps.
On the outside, blend it smooth or leave the snakes showing — your choice.
ask: How do I roll snakes that don't flatten?

video.title: Watch how to build with clay snakes

title: 5. Roll a flat tile
plain: Roll the clay like cookie dough, then cut a tile or a small plate.
why: Even thickness keeps a flat piece from curling as it dries.
doneWhen: The tile is the same thickness everywhere and lies flat.
body: Roll between two sticks of the same height so it is even. Press both sides. Cut the shape. Dry it slowly or the edges curl.
steps: Put two sticks of the same height on either side of the clay.
Roll until the rolling pin rides on the sticks — now the clay is even.
Flip it. Press both faces with the back of a spoon.
Cut your tile. Wait until it feels firm, like a leather belt, before adding stamps or drawing.
Cover it with a plastic bag first, then uncover a little each day.
ask: Why did my tile curl up while drying?

title: 6. Let air-dry clay dry slowly
plain: Air-dry clay hardens on a shelf. It shrinks a little as water leaves. If one part dries faster than another, it cracks. Slow is safer than a hairdryer or oven.
why: Most beginner cracks happen in the first two days of drying, not while you are making the piece.
doneWhen: The piece is lighter in color all over, no longer cool or damp, and a gentle tap sounds sharp — not dull.
body: Keep the sides even. Cover loosely with plastic, then uncover over days. Flip it so the bottom can dry too. Do not use a hairdryer or oven.
steps: Check that no part is much thicker than another.
Set it on cardboard or baking paper — not a sealed plastic plate.
Cover loosely with a plastic bag for the first day so it dries slowly.
Open the bag a little each day. Flip the piece so the bottom dries too.
Leave it 2–4 days for a small bowl. Thick pieces can take a week.
Do not use a hairdryer, heater, sunny windowsill, or oven.

terms.meaning: Clay that hardens at room temperature. No kiln, no oven.

title: 7. If something went wrong
plain: Most beginner problems are water, air bubbles, or a weak join — not a lack of talent.
why: Naming the cause makes the next piece easier. You did not 'ruin' clay. You learned what it needed.
doneWhen: You can point to one cause (too wet, too fast, skipped scratching) and know what to try next.
body: Crack in the bottom: the base was not pressed firm. Edges curl: it dried too fast. Handle pops off: you skipped scratching. Sides collapse: the clay was too wet.
steps: Crack across the bottom → next time, press the inside of the base firmly with your thumb.
Edges curl → cover with a bag and dry slower.
Handle pops off → scratch, add clay-water paste, and smooth the join. Don't skip the scratching.
Sides collapse → the clay was too wet. Wait 10 minutes and try again.
ask: My bowl cracked on the bottom. What did I do wrong?
